newsitem.title: UK: Clashes as police take over N. Ireland march route.
newsitem.headline: Clashes as police take over N. Ireland march route.

text.p: Troops and police seized control of the route of a Protestant parade before dawn on Sunday, clashing with Catholic residents who feared the move meant the march would be forced through their area.

Residents threw rocks and petrol bombs at the security forces and several people were injured by plastic bullets hours before the Orange Order parade, one of the most divisive in Northern Ireland's history, was due to start, witnesses said.

Police and the British government refused to say whether the action meant the march would go through the Garvaghy Road Catholic enclave of Portadown but said that a statement would be made in the next few hours. "We are putting in place measures that will assist us to police a parade later in the day," a police spokesman said.
"The decision to intervene in this way has been taken only with the greatest reluctance and in light of our very real fears of serious violence," the spokesman added.

He refused to say whether marchers of the Protestant Orange Order would be allowed to follow their traditional route along the Garvaghy Road, where residents resent the parade as an annual display of sectarian intimidation.
Residents said they believed the police action meant the security forces would try to force either the full parade or a token march down the road in coming hours.
A spokesman for Britain's Northern Ireland office told Reuters. "I think we will be making a statement in the next few hours."
British troops threw a cordon of barbed wire around nearby Drumcree Anglican church, where the Orange Order traditionally stops for prayers before marching back to Portadown along Garvaghy Road.
Then police in armoured jeeps took control of Garvaghy Road itself, coming under an hour-long attack from residents who had mounted an overnight picket, witnesses said.

Skirmishes continued along side streets as youths pelted riot police with anything they could lay their hands on but as dawn arrived police had taken control of the pole-straight road with hundreds of armoured jeeps parked bumper to bumper.
Several residents were injured by plastic bullets fired by police. "This is brute force," a middle-aged woman screamed at the police.
One of the injured was a woman who went to the aid of a middle-aged man who had been struck by one of the rounds, witnesses said. She was carried to an ambulance screaming in pain.

A local nun, a member of the Garvaghy Road residents committee, said she was furious at Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, for failing to say publicly what decision had been taken over the parade route.

"Mo Mowlam promised us she would let us know what the decision was, no matter what time of the night, and she didn't. She has really betrayed us. I've lost trust in her. We have been treated like dirt," Sister Laura Boyle told Reuters.
One year ago police prevented the marchers going through the Catholic enclave but changed their decision after days of Protestant rioting and sparked Catholic fury instead.

Dozens more Protestant parades are to be staged this week in the build-up to the 12th of July, the most cherished date in the Orange calendar which marks a 17th century Protestant victory over Britain's last Catholic king.

This year's planned march has confronted Britain's new Labour government with its first major political test of pledges to give equal rights to the pro-British Protestant majority and pro-Irish Catholic minority.
